decks.title: Some Basic Concepts — Part 1: Chemistry, measurement and dimensional analysis
goals: Give examples of the role of chemistry in medicine, agriculture, industry and the environment
Distinguish precision from accuracy and report results with the right number of significant figures
Convert between units with conversion factors, for example litre to cubic metre and atmosphere to pascal

slides.heading: Chemistry, Measurement and Units
slides.body_md: Part 1: what chemistry does for us, how matter is classified, and how chemists measure and convert quantities honestly.

visual.alt: Table of areas where chemistry is applied with an example for each

slides.narration: Welcome to the first chapter of Class Eleven chemistry. Chemistry sits behind the medicines in a hospital, the fertiliser in a field, the cement in a building and the filters that clean our water. In this part we see the scope of chemistry, how matter is classified, how measurements are reported with care, and how units are converted with confidence.

slides.heading: Scope of chemistry
slides.body_md: Chemistry studies the **composition, structure, properties and changes** of matter. It links physics and biology and supports every industry.

rows: Designs and purifies drugs; develops diagnostic tests
Supplies nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium fertilisers; plant protection chemicals
Produces metals, polymers, glass, soaps and fuels
Monitors pollutants; develops green processes that cut waste

visual.alt: Table of fields and the role chemistry plays in each

slides.narration: Chemistry studies what matter is made of, how it is built, what properties it has and how it changes. In medicine, chemists design and purify drugs. In agriculture they supply fertilisers and test soils. Industry depends on chemistry for metals, plastics, glass and soaps. And in the environment, chemistry measures pollution and develops greener processes that produce less waste.

slides.heading: Classification of matter
slides.body_md: A **pure substance** has fixed composition: an **element** (one kind of atom) or a **compound** (different atoms combined in a fixed mass ratio). A **mixture** has variable composition and can be separated by physical methods.

visual.alt: Flow chart classifying matter into pure substances and mixtures, and each into two kinds

slides.narration: All matter is either a pure substance or a mixture. A pure substance has a fixed composition and is either an element, made of one kind of atom, or a compound, in which different atoms are combined in a fixed ratio by mass. A mixture has variable composition. It is homogeneous when uniform throughout, like brass or sugar solution, and heterogeneous when different parts can be seen.

slides.heading: SI units and scientific notation
slides.body_md: Seven SI base units; derived units are built from them. Write numbers as $N \times 10^{n}$ with $1 \le N < 10$.

visual.alt: Table of SI quantities with their units and expressions in base units

slides.narration: The International System of units has seven base units, including the metre, the kilogram, the kelvin and the mole. Every other unit is built from them. The pascal for pressure and the joule for energy are derived units. Very large and very small values are written in scientific notation, a number between one and ten multiplied by a power of ten. The litre is not an SI unit.

slides.heading: Precision and accuracy
slides.body_md: **Precision**: repeated readings agree with one another. **Accuracy**: readings, or their mean, agree with the true value. A **systematic error** shifts all readings the same way.

visual.caption: Closeness of dots to each other is precision; closeness to the dashed line is accuracy.

slides.narration: Look at the three students reading a twenty five millilitre standard. Student one is both precise and accurate. Student two has readings that agree with each other but sit above the true value, so precise but not accurate, which suggests a systematic error. Student three is scattered, not precise, although the mean happens to fall near the true value.

slides.heading: Worked example: percentage error
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Using the true value 25.00 mL, find the percentage error of the mean for students 2 and 3 of the plot (readings 25.58, 25.62, 25.66 and 24.40, 25.85, 25.10 mL).

**Student 2.** Mean $= (25.58 + 25.62 + 25.66)/3 = 25.62$ mL. Error $= 0.62$ mL, so percentage error $= 0.62 / 25.00 \times 100 = 2.5\ \%$.

**Student 3.** Mean $= (24.40 + 25.85 + 25.10)/3 = 25.12$ mL. Error $= 0.12$ mL, so percentage error $= 0.12 / 25.00 \times 100 \approx 0.5\ \%$. Yet the readings span 1.45 mL: the mean is accurate by luck, not by good technique.

visual.alt: Table comparing mean, spread and percentage error for students 2 and 3

slides.narration: Percentage error is the absolute error divided by the true value, times one hundred. Student two has a mean that is more than half a millilitre too high, about two and a half percent, but very small spread. Student three has a small error in the mean, about half a percent, but a spread of nearly one and a half millilitres. Accuracy of the mean alone does not prove good technique.

slides.heading: Quick check: precision and accuracy
slides.body_md: Read the three sets of balance readings and judge each.
slides.narration: Quick check. Three trainee analysts have each weighed the same certified mass. First compare how close the readings of each trainee are to one another, which shows precision. Then compare the mean of each set with the certified value, which shows accuracy. Decide which trainee is both.

slides.heading: Significant figures: counting
slides.body_md: Significant figures are the digits known with certainty plus one estimated digit.

rows: Trailing zeros after a decimal point count
In scientific notation all coefficient digits count

visual.alt: Table of the rules for counting significant figures with examples

slides.narration: Count significant figures with a few rules. Non-zero digits always count. Zeros between non-zero digits count. Leading zeros do not count, they only place the decimal point. Trailing zeros count when they come after a decimal point. In scientific notation, every digit in the coefficient counts. Exact numbers, such as counts and defined conversion factors, have unlimited significant figures.

slides.heading: Significant figures in calculations
slides.body_md: **Add or subtract:** keep the **fewest decimal places**. **Multiply or divide:** keep the **fewest significant figures**. Round only at the final step.

nodes.label: Add or subtract: match the fewest decimal places
Multiply or divide: match the fewest significant figures
Keep an extra digit in between and round once at the end

visual.alt: Flow showing which significant-figure rule to apply and when to round

slides.narration: When you add or subtract, the answer keeps as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places. When you multiply or divide, the answer keeps as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest. Carry one extra digit through the middle of a calculation and round only once at the end, so that rounding errors do not pile up.

slides.heading: Worked example: significant figures
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Report each result correctly. (a) $7.805 + 0.34 + 12.1$ (b) $\dfrac{0.0820 \times 15.6}{2.5}$ (c) Write $0.000306$ in scientific notation.

**(a)** Sum $= 20.245$; 12.1 has one decimal place, so the answer is $20.2$.

**(b)** $0.0820 \times 15.6 = 1.2792$ and $1.2792 / 2.5 = 0.51168$. The fewest significant figures is two (2.5), so the answer is $0.51$.

**(c)** $0.000306 = 3.06 \times 10^{-4}$ (three significant figures).

visual.alt: Table of the three significant-figure answers and the rule for each

slides.narration: In part a, the term with the fewest decimal places is twelve point one, so the sum is rounded to one decimal place. In part b, the divisor has only two significant figures, so the answer has two. In part c, moving the decimal point four places to the right gives ten to the minus four, keeping all three significant figures.

slides.heading: Quick check: significant figures
slides.body_md: Apply the correct rule to a density calculation.
slides.narration: Quick check. A density is found by dividing a mass by a volume. Count the significant figures in each measured value before you divide, remember the rule for division, and then choose the option that has the correct number of digits. Do not round until the very end.

slides.heading: Dimensional analysis: the factor-label method
slides.body_md: A **conversion factor** is a ratio equal to 1, such as $\dfrac{101325\ \text{Pa}}{1\ \text{atm}}$. Multiply by it so that the unwanted unit cancels.

nodes.label: Write the quantity with its unit
Choose a factor equal to 1 that cancels the old unit
Check the unit and the significant figures

visual.alt: Flow of the factor-label method for converting units

slides.narration: Dimensional analysis converts units with conversion factors. A conversion factor is a ratio of two equal quantities written in different units, so it equals one and does not change the size of the quantity. Choose the factor so the unit you want to remove cancels, multiply, and then check that the unit left is the one you need and that the significant figures are right.

slides.heading: Worked example: unit conversion
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Convert (a) 3.6 L to m³, (b) 0.75 atm to Pa (1 atm $= 101325$ Pa), (c) 90 km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹.

**(a)** $3.6\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3}{1\ \text{L}} = 3.6 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$.

**(b)** $0.75 \times 101325 = 75993.75 \approx 7.6 \times 10^{4}$ Pa (two significant figures).

**(c)** $90 \times \dfrac{1000}{3600} = 25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$.

rows: 1000 m per km, 3600 s per h

visual.alt: Table of three unit conversions with the factor used and the result

slides.narration: For the volume, one litre equals ten to the minus three cubic metres, so three point six litres is three point six times ten to the minus three cubic metres. For the pressure, multiply by one hundred and one thousand three hundred and twenty five pascal per atmosphere and keep two significant figures. For the speed, multiply by one thousand metres per kilometre and divide by three thousand six hundred seconds per hour.

slides.body_md: Volume units are cubes of length units, so each step between m³, dm³ and cm³ is a factor of $10^{3}$, not 10.

slides.narration: Because volume is length cubed, the step from a cubic metre to a cubic decimetre is not ten but one thousand, since ten decimetres make a metre and ten cubed is one thousand. A litre is the same as a cubic decimetre, and a millilitre is the same as a cubic centimetre. Moving right multiplies by one thousand; moving left divides.

slides.heading: Applications of dimensional analysis
slides.body_md: Dimensions let us (1) **convert** units, (2) **check** whether an equation is homogeneous, and (3) **find the unit** of a constant. For example $R = \dfrac{PV}{nT}$ has units $\dfrac{\text{Pa m}^3}{\text{mol K}} = \text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$.

rows: atm to Pa, L to m³
Both sides of $PV = nRT$ must be in energy units
Adding a mass to a volume is impossible

visual.alt: Table of applications of dimensional analysis

slides.narration: Dimensional analysis does more than convert units. It checks that an equation makes sense, because every term must have the same dimensions. It also tells us the unit of a constant: pressure times volume divided by amount and temperature gives joules per kelvin per mole for the gas constant. And it catches errors, since a mass cannot be added to a volume.

slides.heading: Worked example: pressure times volume
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A gas at 2.0 atm occupies 5.0 L. Express $PV$ in joules, using 1 L $= 10^{-3}$ m³ and 1 atm $= 101325$ Pa.

$P = 2.0 \times 101325 = 202650$ Pa; $V = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ m³.

$PV = 202650 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-3} = 1013$ Pa m³ $= 1013$ J $\approx 1.0 \times 10^{3}$ J (two significant figures).

visual.alt: Table of the steps converting litre atmospheres into joules

slides.narration: Convert both quantities to base units first. Two atmospheres is about two hundred thousand pascal and five litres is five times ten to the minus three cubic metres. Their product is about one thousand pascal cubic metres, which is exactly one thousand joules, because a pascal times a cubic metre is a newton times a metre, which is a joule.

slides.heading: Quick check: units
slides.body_md: Convert a gauge reading from pascal to atmospheres.
slides.narration: Quick check. The gauge reads in pascal but the answer is wanted in atmospheres. Choose the conversion factor so that the unit pascal cancels and atmosphere remains, then divide carefully. Keep two significant figures, because the reading has two.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Matter: pure substances (elements, compounds) and mixtures (homogeneous, heterogeneous).
Precision is agreement among readings; accuracy is agreement with the true value.
Add and subtract: fewest decimal places. Multiply and divide: fewest significant figures.
Conversion factors equal 1; volume steps between m³, dm³ and cm³ are $10^{3}$.
Dimensional analysis converts units, checks equations and gives units of constants.

visual.alt: Summary table of tools from Part 1

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Matter is classified into pure substances and mixtures. Precision is about agreement among readings and accuracy about agreement with the truth. Use the decimal place rule for sums and the significant figure rule for products. Convert units with factors equal to one, remembering that volume steps are factors of one thousand. Dimensions also check equations.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write units in every step of a conversion and cancel them visibly.
Quote answers to the correct number of significant figures; round at the end.
Use the true value (not the measured one) in the denominator of percentage error.
A litre is a dm³, not a m³.
Defined conversion factors are exact; they never limit significant figures.

rows: Percent error divided by the measured value

visual.alt: Table of common slips from Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Exam tips for Part 1. Write the units in every line and cancel them. Round only at the very end, and use the right number of significant figures. For percentage error, divide by the true value. Remember that one litre is one thousandth of a cubic metre, and that defined conversion factors are exact and never reduce your significant figures.

decks.title: Some Basic Concepts — Part 2: Laws of chemical combination and Dalton’s theory
goals: State each law of chemical combination and verify it from experimental data
Solve problems on Gay-Lussac’s law of combining volumes
Explain how Dalton’s theory accounts for the laws and state its limitations

slides.heading: Laws of Chemical Combination
slides.body_md: Part 2: five quantitative laws, the simple volume law for gases, and the atomic theory that explained them.

visual.alt: Table of the laws of chemical combination with their proposers and years

slides.narration: This part covers the laws that came from careful weighing and measuring. Lavoisier showed mass is conserved. Proust found fixed composition. Richter found the reciprocal proportions. Dalton found multiple proportions, and Gay-Lussac found simple ratios of gas volumes. Then we see how Dalton’s atomic theory explains the first four, and why it needed to be extended.

slides.heading: Law of conservation of mass
slides.body_md: In a chemical reaction the **total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products**. Atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed. The law holds only if every substance, including gases, is counted.

slides.narration: Lavoisier’s law says that in any chemical change, the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. Here, four point eight grams of magnesium and three point two grams of oxygen make eight grams of magnesium oxide. The two bars have the same height. Apparent losses or gains in open vessels come from gases that entered or escaped.

slides.heading: Worked example: conservation of mass
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** In a closed tube, 5.60 g of iron powder and 3.20 g of sulfur react to form iron(II) sulfide, $\ce{Fe + S -> FeS}$. (a) What mass of iron(II) sulfide forms? (b) If 6.00 g of iron is used with 3.20 g of sulfur, what mass of iron remains, assuming the same mass of FeS forms?

**(a)** Mass of product $= 5.60 + 3.20 = 8.80$ g.

**(b)** The product is still 8.80 g, which uses 5.60 g of iron, so the iron left is $6.00 - 5.60 = 0.40$ g.

visual.alt: Table of masses of iron, sulfur and iron sulfide in two experiments

slides.narration: In a closed tube nothing escapes, so the mass of iron sulfide equals the sum of the masses of iron and sulfur, eight point eight grams. In the second experiment extra iron is added. The sulfur still reacts only with the same mass of iron, the same eight point eight grams of product forms, and the surplus four tenths of a gram of iron is left unreacted.

slides.heading: Law of definite proportions
slides.body_md: A pure compound always contains the **same elements in the same proportion by mass**, whatever its source or method of preparation (Proust).

visual.alt: Table showing the same oxygen to hydrogen mass ratio in three samples of water

slides.narration: Proust showed that a pure compound always contains the same elements in the same mass ratio, no matter where it came from or how it was made. Water from a tap, from rain or distilled from the sea always has eight parts of oxygen to one part of hydrogen by mass. Different ratios would mean a different compound or an impure sample.

slides.heading: Law of multiple proportions
slides.body_md: When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a **fixed mass** of the other are in a **simple whole-number ratio** (Dalton).

headers: O combined with 1.00 g N / g

visual.alt: Table of four nitrogen oxides with oxygen masses per gram of nitrogen in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3 : 4

slides.narration: Nitrogen forms several oxides. Fix the mass of nitrogen at one gram and compare the masses of oxygen. They come out as point five seven, one point one four, one point seven one and two point two nine grams, in the simple ratio one to two to three to four. Whole-number ratios like these are what Dalton’s atoms in whole-number combinations would predict.

slides.heading: Quick check: conservation of mass
slides.body_md: Use the law to find the mass of an unknown product.
slides.narration: Quick check. In a sealed vessel the total mass is unchanged by the reaction. Add up the masses of the two reactants, then subtract the mass of the product that is already known, and what remains must be the mass of the other product.

slides.heading: Worked example: multiple proportions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Copper forms two oxides. Oxide A is 88.8 % copper and oxide B is 79.9 % copper by mass. Show that the data obey the law of multiple proportions.

Oxide A: oxygen $= 100 - 88.8 = 11.2$ g per 88.8 g Cu, so $11.2 / 88.8 = 0.126$ g O per gram of Cu.

Oxide B: oxygen $= 100 - 79.9 = 20.1$ g per 79.9 g Cu, so $20.1 / 79.9 = 0.252$ g O per gram of Cu.

Ratio $0.126 : 0.252 = 1 : 2$. The data obey the law (A is $\ce{Cu2O}$, B is $\ce{CuO}$).

visual.alt: Table of percentage composition and oxygen per gram of copper for two copper oxides

slides.narration: Start from the percentage composition. Treat the percentages as grams in a hundred gram sample, subtract to get the oxygen, and divide by the copper to get oxygen per gram of copper. The values point one two six and point two five two are in the ratio one to two, a simple whole number ratio, so the law of multiple proportions holds.

slides.heading: Law of reciprocal proportions
slides.body_md: If two elements combine separately with a fixed mass of a third, they combine with each other in the **same ratio or a simple multiple** of it (Richter).

slides.narration: Richter’s law links three elements. In hydrogen sulfide, one gram of hydrogen takes sixteen grams of sulfur. In water, one gram of hydrogen takes eight grams of oxygen. So through hydrogen, sulfur to oxygen is two to one. In sulfur dioxide the direct ratio is one to one, which is one half of that, a simple fraction, so the law holds.

slides.heading: Worked example: reciprocal proportions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Methane has 12.0 g C with 4.00 g H; carbon disulfide has 12.0 g C with 64.0 g S; hydrogen sulfide has 1.00 g H with 16.0 g S. Test the law of reciprocal proportions.

Through carbon: H : S $= 4.00 : 64.0 = 1 : 16$.

Directly, in hydrogen sulfide: H : S $= 1.00 : 16.0 = 1 : 16$.

The ratios are identical (a simple multiple of 1), so the law is obeyed.

visual.alt: Table comparing the hydrogen to sulfur ratio through carbon with the direct ratio

slides.narration: Fix the mass of carbon at twelve grams. It combines with four grams of hydrogen in methane and with sixty four grams of sulfur in carbon disulfide, so hydrogen to sulfur through carbon is one to sixteen. In hydrogen sulfide, hydrogen and sulfur combine directly in the ratio one to sixteen. The ratios agree exactly, so the data verify the law.

slides.heading: Quick check: reciprocal proportions
slides.body_md: Compare the ratio through a common element with the direct ratio.
slides.narration: Quick check. Look at the three sets of masses. First find the ratio of nitrogen to oxygen through the common element hydrogen, using the same mass of hydrogen in both compounds. Then compare it with the ratio of nitrogen to oxygen in the oxide itself.

slides.heading: Gay-Lussac’s law of combining volumes
slides.body_md: Gases react in **simple whole-number ratios by volume**, and form gaseous products in simple ratios, at the same temperature and pressure. The law applies to gases only.

slides.narration: Gay-Lussac measured gas volumes. One volume of nitrogen and three volumes of hydrogen give two volumes of ammonia, all at the same temperature and pressure. The ratio one to three to two is a simple whole number ratio. The law applies to gases only, and the volumes of liquids and solids do not follow such ratios.

slides.heading: Worked example: combining volumes
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 10 mL of ethane is burnt in 50 mL of oxygen: $\ce{2C2H6 + 7O2 -> 4CO2 + 6H2O}$. After cooling to the original temperature and pressure (water liquid), find the volume of each gas left.

Volumes react as $2 : 7 : 4$. O₂ used $= 10 \times 7/2 = 35$ mL; CO₂ formed $= 10 \times 4/2 = 20$ mL; O₂ left $= 50 - 35 = 15$ mL.

Total gas $= 20 + 15 = 35$ mL; shaking with alkali removes the CO₂, leaving 15 mL.

visual.alt: Table of gas volumes before and after the combustion of ethane

slides.narration: Use the volume ratio from the balanced equation: two ethane, seven oxygen, four carbon dioxide. Ten millilitres of ethane needs thirty five of oxygen and gives twenty of carbon dioxide. Oxygen left is fifteen, so thirty five millilitres of gas remain after the water condenses. Passing the gas through alkali removes the carbon dioxide and leaves fifteen millilitres of oxygen.

slides.heading: Dalton’s atomic theory
slides.body_md: Matter is made of **indivisible atoms**; atoms of one element are **identical in mass and properties** and differ from atoms of other elements; atoms combine in **small whole-number ratios**; reactions only **rearrange** atoms.

rows: Atoms are not created or destroyed
Compound atoms combine in a fixed whole-number ratio; atoms of an element have fixed mass
The same atoms may combine in more than one whole-number ratio
Atoms are the units that combine

visual.alt: Table linking each postulate of Dalton’s theory to the law it explains

slides.narration: Dalton proposed that matter is made of tiny indivisible atoms. Atoms of one element are alike, atoms of different elements differ, and atoms combine in small whole numbers to form compounds. In a reaction they are only rearranged. These ideas explain the laws of conservation of mass, definite proportions, multiple proportions and reciprocal proportions.

slides.heading: Limitations of Dalton’s theory
slides.body_md: Later discoveries showed that several postulates need revision.

rows: Electrons, protons and neutrons were found inside atoms
Atoms of an element are identical in mass

visual.alt: Table of limitations of Dalton’s theory with the discoveries that contradict them

slides.narration: Dalton’s theory was a great step but has limits. Atoms are divisible, since electrons, protons and neutrons exist inside them. Atoms of one element can differ in mass, as isotopes do. Treating the smallest particle of a gas as an atom could not explain Gay-Lussac’s volumes. And diamond and graphite, both carbon, differ widely in properties.

slides.heading: Quick check: limitations
slides.body_md: Choose the observation that contradicts a Dalton postulate.
slides.narration: Quick check. Dalton said that all atoms of one element are identical in mass. Ask which of the four observations shows that atoms of a single element can differ in mass, and which are only the laws that his theory successfully explained.

slides.heading: Avogadro’s molecule
slides.body_md: **Avogadro (1811):** equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of **molecules**; molecules of hydrogen and chlorine are **diatomic**.

visual.alt: Equation of hydrogen and chlorine forming two molecules of hydrogen chloride
visual.caption: One volume of hydrogen and one of chlorine give two volumes of hydrogen chloride.

slides.narration: Avogadro solved the puzzle of the volumes. If equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules, and hydrogen and chlorine molecules each contain two atoms, then one molecule of each makes two molecules of hydrogen chloride, which is one volume plus one volume giving two volumes. The idea of the molecule extended Dalton’s atom.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Conservation of mass; definite proportions; multiple proportions; reciprocal proportions.
To test a law from measurements, compare ratios of masses at a fixed mass of one element.
Gay-Lussac: simple whole-number volume ratios for gases at the same T and P.
Dalton’s postulates explain the mass laws.
Limitations: divisible atoms, isotopes, diatomic gas molecules, allotropes.

rows: Fix one element, ratio of the other

visual.alt: Summary table of laws and how each is tested

slides.narration: To sum up Part 2. Mass is conserved. A compound has a fixed composition. Two elements that form several compounds do so in whole number mass ratios. Two elements that combine with a third combine with each other in the same ratio or a simple multiple. Gases combine in simple volume ratios. Dalton’s atoms explain the mass laws, and his theory needed Avogadro’s molecule and the discovery of subatomic particles.

For multiple proportions fix the mass of one element, then compare the other.
For reciprocal proportions compare the ratio through the third element with the direct ratio.
For gas volumes write the balanced equation first; remember liquid water has negligible volume.
Give a specific example for each limitation of Dalton’s theory.

Convert to grams per gram of one element
Counting liquid water as a gas volume
Treat condensed water as zero volume

slides.narration: Exam tips for Part 2. Always name the law you are verifying and show the ratio. For multiple proportions fix one element, for reciprocal proportions use a third element, and compare the ratios. For gas volumes start from the balanced equation, and do not count liquid water as a gas. When asked for limitations of Dalton’s theory, give a specific piece of evidence for each.

notes.title: Some Basic Concepts: Measurement, Laws of Chemical Combination and Atomic Theory — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Scope of chemistry and classification of matter
sections.body_md:
Chemistry studies the composition, structure, properties and changes of matter. It contributes to **medicine** (drugs, diagnostics), **agriculture** (fertilisers, soil testing), **industry** (metals, polymers, glass, soaps, fuels) and the **environment** (monitoring pollutants, green processes).

Matter is a **pure substance** (fixed composition) or a **mixture** (variable composition, separable by physical methods). A pure substance is an **element** (one kind of atom) or a **compound** (different atoms combined in a fixed ratio by mass, separable only by chemical methods). A mixture is **homogeneous** (uniform, such as brass) or **heterogeneous** (visibly different parts, such as oil and water).

key_terms.definition_md: A pure substance made of one kind of atom that cannot be split chemically.
A pure substance of two or more elements combined in a fixed mass ratio.
A mixture with uniform composition throughout.
A mixture whose parts can be seen and separated physically.

visual.alt: Flow chart classifying matter

sections.heading: 2. Precision, accuracy and significant figures
sections.body_md:
**Precision** is the closeness of repeated measurements to one another; **accuracy** is the closeness of a measurement, or of the mean, to the true value. **Percentage error** $= \dfrac{|\text{measured} - \text{true}|}{\text{true}} \times 100$.

**Significant figures:** non-zero digits and zeros between them count; leading zeros do not; trailing zeros count after a decimal point; all coefficient digits count in scientific notation. **Add or subtract:** keep the fewest decimal places. **Multiply or divide:** keep the fewest significant figures. Exact numbers have unlimited significant figures. Round only at the end.

key_terms.definition_md: The digits of a measurement that are known reliably, plus one estimated digit.
Agreement of repeated readings with one another.
Agreement of a reading or mean with the true value.
An error that shifts all readings the same way, for example a zero error.

sections.heading: 3. SI units and dimensional analysis
sections.body_md:
The SI base units are metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. Derived units: newton $= \text{kg m s}^{-2}$, pascal $= \text{kg m}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-2}$, joule $= \text{kg m}^{2}\text{ s}^{-2}$. The litre ($1\ \text{dm}^3 = 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$) is not an SI unit.

**Dimensional analysis** converts units with **conversion factors equal to 1**: for example $1\ \text{atm} = 101325\ \text{Pa}$, $1\ \text{L} = 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$, $1\ \text{nm} = 10^{-9}\ \text{m}$. Volume units step by $10^{3}$ (m³, dm³, cm³). It also checks that equations are homogeneous and gives units of constants, for example $R = PV/(nT)$ in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, and shows that $1\ \text{L atm} = 101.3\ \text{J}$.

key_terms.definition_md: A ratio of equal quantities in different units, equal to 1.
A unit built from base units, such as the pascal or joule.
Using units to convert quantities, check equations and find units of constants.

sections.heading: 4. Conservation of mass, definite and multiple proportions
sections.body_md:
- **Conservation of mass** (Lavoisier): total mass of reactants equals total mass of products; count every substance, including gases.
- **Definite (constant) proportions** (Proust): a pure compound always has the same elements in the same mass ratio. Test: two samples give the same mass fraction.
- **Multiple proportions** (Dalton): when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio. Test: fix one element at 1.00 g and compare the other (for example $\ce{Cu2O}$ and $\ce{CuO}$ give 1 : 2).

key_terms.definition_md: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
A compound has fixed composition by mass.
Masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of another are in a simple whole-number ratio.

sections.heading: 5. Reciprocal proportions and Gay-Lussac’s law
sections.body_md:
**Reciprocal proportions** (Richter): if A and B each combine with a fixed mass of C, then A and B combine with each other in the same ratio or a simple multiple of it. Example: through hydrogen S : O $= 16 : 8 = 2 : 1$; in $\ce{SO2}$ the ratio is 1 : 1, half of this.

**Gay-Lussac’s law:** gases react, and form gaseous products, in simple whole-number volume ratios when measured at the same temperature and pressure. The volume ratio equals the coefficient ratio of the balanced equation: $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$ is $1 : 3 : 2$. **Avogadro’s law:** equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules; it explains why hydrogen and chlorine are diatomic. Liquid water is taken to have negligible volume.

key_terms.definition_md: Two elements combine with each other in the ratio, or a simple multiple of the ratio, in which they combine with a third element.
Gaseous volumes react in simple whole-number ratios at constant temperature and pressure.
Equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules.

sections.heading: 6. Dalton’s atomic theory and its limitations
sections.body_md:
**Postulates:** matter consists of indivisible atoms; atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties; atoms of different elements differ; compounds form by combination of atoms in small whole-number ratios; atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed, in reactions.

**Explains:** conservation of mass (no atoms lost), definite proportions (fixed atom ratio of fixed-mass atoms), multiple proportions (same atoms in different whole-number ratios) and reciprocal proportions.

**Limitations:** atoms are divisible (electron, proton, neutron); atoms of an element can differ in mass (isotopes); it treated gas particles as atoms and so could not explain Gay-Lussac’s law (molecules, Avogadro); it cannot explain allotropes (diamond and graphite).

key_terms.definition_md: The smallest particle of an element that takes part in chemical change.
A group of atoms bonded together that can exist independently.
Atoms of the same element with different masses.

rows: Atoms are not created or destroyed

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Rounding in the middle of a calculation or quoting too many significant figures.
- Dividing percentage error by the measured value instead of the true value.
- Taking 1 L as 10⁻⁶ m³, or using a factor of 10 instead of 10³ between cubic units.
- Verifying a law without stating the ratio and the law's name.
- Treating liquid water as a gas when finding the volume after combustion.
- Calling reciprocal proportions multiple proportions.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a definition, a single conversion or a significant-figure count.
- Verification of a law (2–3 marks): per-gram masses (1), simple ratio (1), law named and stated (1).
- Gas-volume problems: volume ratio from the balanced equation (1), each volume (1), total or leftover gas (1).
- Limitations of Dalton's theory: each limitation with its evidence (1).

questions.stem_md: A food-technology student sorts samples from a school canteen. Which of these is a heterogeneous mixture?

options.text_md: sugar fully dissolved in hot tea
filtered air from the canteen kitchen
mustard oil shaken with water, photographed a minute after shaking
a pinch of iodised salt stirred into a glass of water

questions.solution_md: Oil and water form visible separate phases, so the mixture is heterogeneous — option (c). The other three samples are uniform throughout, which makes them homogeneous mixtures (solutions).

questions.stem_md: A white crystalline solid melts at 801 °C. Electrolysis of the molten solid gives a silvery metal at one electrode and a pale-green gas at the other, and neither product can be broken down further by chemical means. The solid is best classified as:

options.text_md: an element, because it is a pure substance
a homogeneous mixture, because it is uniform
a heterogeneous mixture, because two products form
a compound, because it splits into two different elements by electrolysis

questions.solution_md: A pure substance that can be decomposed chemically into simpler substances of fixed composition is a compound — option (d). It is pure, but a pure substance can be an element or a compound (a); a mixture can be separated by physical methods, not by electrolysis (b, c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A solution of ethanol in water is a compound, because its particles are uniformly distributed throughout.
questions.solution_md: False. Uniform distribution only shows the mixture is homogeneous. A compound has a fixed composition by mass and cannot be separated by physical methods, whereas ethanol and water can be separated by distillation and the solution can have any composition.

questions.stem_md: A mixture whose composition and properties are uniform throughout, such as brass, is called a ___ mixture.
questions.solution_md: Uniform composition throughout means a **homogeneous** mixture, as in an alloy or a solution; a heterogeneous mixture has visibly different parts.

questions.stem_md: A district health officer and an agricultural extension worker both depend on chemistry. Give one specific contribution of chemistry to medicine and one to agriculture.

answer.model_answer_md: Medicine: chemists synthesise and purify drugs, for example antibiotics such as penicillin derivatives, and design vaccines and diagnostic reagents. Agriculture: chemistry provides fertilisers rich in nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and pesticides and soil-testing methods that raise crop yields.

questions.solution_md: One specific example from each area.

questions.stem_md: Classify each of the following as an element, a compound, a homogeneous mixture or a heterogeneous mixture, giving one reason: (i) the graphite of a pencil lead, (ii) baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate), (iii) river sand mixed with iron filings.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Graphite is an element: it consists of carbon atoms only and cannot be broken down chemically. (ii) Sodium hydrogencarbonate is a compound: it contains sodium, hydrogen, carbon and oxygen combined in a fixed mass ratio and can be decomposed chemically. (iii) Sand with iron filings is a heterogeneous mixture: the two solids are visible as separate parts and a magnet separates the iron.

questions.solution_md: Element, compound, heterogeneous mixture, each with a reason.

questions.stem_md: Three trainee analysts each weigh a certified 20.000 g standard mass three times. Trainee X records 20.31, 20.3, 20.32 g, trainee Y records 20.00, 19.99, 20.01 g and trainee Z records 19.6, 20.5, 20.0 g. Which statement is correct?

options.text_md: Only Y is both precise and accurate.
X is both precise and accurate.
Z is precise but not accurate.
X is accurate but not precise.

questions.solution_md: X: readings agree closely (precise) but the mean 20.31 g is about 0.31 g too high (not accurate). Y: readings within 0.02 g of each other and a mean of 20.00 g (precise and accurate). Z: readings spread over 0.9 g (not precise), although the mean 20.03 g is near the true value. Only Y is both — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The mass of a liquid sample is measured as 21.35 g and its volume as 25.0 mL. The density should be reported, in g mL⁻¹, as:
questions.solution_md: Division keeps the fewest significant figures. The mass has four, the volume three, so the density has three: $21.35 / 25.0 = 0.8540 \approx 0.854$ g mL⁻¹ — option (d). (a) keeps four figures, (b) two and (c) one.

questions.stem_md: The numbers of significant figures in $3.040$, $0.00205$ and $5.0 \times 10^{-4}$ are, respectively:
questions.solution_md: $3.040$: the zero after the decimal point is significant, so 4. $0.00205$: leading zeros are not significant but the zero between 2 and 5 is, so 3. $5.0 \times 10^{-4}$: both digits of the coefficient count, so 2 — option (a). (b) drops the trailing zero, (c) counts leading zeros, (d) ignores the trailing zero of 5.0.

questions.stem_md: A student lists the SI base units as metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole, candela and litre. The unit wrongly included is:
questions.solution_md: The litre (1 dm³) is a derived, non-SI unit of volume; the SI unit of volume is the cubic metre, built from the base unit metre. Kelvin, mole and ampere are base units — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A standard sodium hydroxide solution is known to be 0.1000 M. A student's titrations give a mean value of 0.1024 M. The percentage error of the student's result is:
questions.solution_md: Percentage error $= \dfrac{|\text{measured} - \text{true}|}{\text{true}} \times 100 = \dfrac{0.1024 - 0.1000}{0.1000} \times 100 \approx 2.4\ \%$ — option (d). (b) divides by the measured value instead of the true value.

questions.stem_md: A virus particle has a diameter of $0.000000085\ \text{m}$. In scientific notation this is:
questions.solution_md: The decimal point moves 8 places to the right to give 8.5, so the power is $-8$: $8.5 \times 10^{-8}$ m — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The product $2.0 \times 3.456$ is reported as $6.9$.

**Reason (R):** In multiplication the result carries the same number of significant figures as the factor that has the fewest.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: $2.0 \times 3.456 = 6.912$. The factor 2.0 has two significant figures, so the result is rounded to $6.9$ — A is true. R states exactly the rule used, so R is the correct explanation — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Pure water distilled from river water and pure water collected from burning hydrogen in air both contain 11.1 % hydrogen by mass.

**Reason (R):** Hydrogen and oxygen form two compounds, $\ce{H2O}$ and $\ce{H2O2}$.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: pure water has a fixed composition (2 × 1 / 18 = 11.1 % hydrogen). R is also true. But the existence of a second compound does not explain why every sample of water has the same composition; the explanation is the law of definite proportions — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student measures the density of ethanol as 0.812 g cm⁻³ at a temperature where the accepted value is 0.789 g cm⁻³. Find the percentage error, to two significant figures.

marking_scheme.step: Absolute error 0.023 divided by the accepted value

questions.stem_md: A chemist mixes three solids of masses 14.236 g, 8.5 g and 0.0612 g. Report the total mass with the correct number of significant figures and state the rule you applied.

answer.model_answer_md: The sum is $14.236 + 8.5 + 0.0612 = 22.7972$ g. In addition the result is given to the same number of decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places; 8.5 g has one, so the total is **22.8 g**.

questions.solution_md: Add, then round to one decimal place.

marking_scheme.step: Rounded to 22.8 g with the decimal-place rule stated

questions.stem_md: A jeweller weighs a 50.00 g test weight three times and records 50.42 g, 50.41 g and 50.43 g. Comment on the precision and accuracy of the balance and suggest the likely kind of error.

answer.model_answer_md: The readings agree within 0.02 g, so the balance is precise. Their mean, 50.42 g, is 0.42 g above the true 50.00 g, so it is not accurate. A steady offset of this kind points to a systematic error, such as a zero error or poor calibration of the balance.

questions.solution_md: Close agreement shows precision; the offset from the true value shows lack of accuracy.

marking_scheme.step: Not accurate, with a systematic error suggested

questions.stem_md: Evaluate each expression and report the result to the correct number of significant figures: (i) $\dfrac{6.25 \times 0.0320}{4.1}$ (ii) $125.5 - 23.74 + 0.065$ (iii) Write the answer to (i) in scientific notation.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) $6.25 \times 0.0320 = 0.2000$ and $0.2000 / 4.1 = 0.0488$; the least precise factor, 4.1, has two significant figures, so the answer is **0.049**. (ii) The sum is $101.825$; 125.5 has one decimal place, so the answer is **101.8**. (iii) $0.049 = 4.9 \times 10^{-2}$.

questions.solution_md: Fewest significant figures for the quotient; fewest decimal places for the sum.

questions.stem_md: A school laboratory weighs a 10.00 g standard five times and records 10.12, 10.15, 10.11, 10.14, 10.13 g. Calculate the mean reading, the absolute error of the mean and the percentage error, and state whether the balance is precise and accurate.

answer.model_answer_md: Mean $= (10.12 + 10.15 + 10.11 + 10.14 + 10.13) / 5 = 10.13$ g. Absolute error $= 10.13 - 10.00 = 0.13$ g. Percentage error $= 0.13 / 10.00 \times 100 = 1.3\ \%$. The readings agree within 0.04 g, so the balance is precise, but the mean is 0.13 g above the true value, so it is not accurate.

questions.solution_md: Mean, error, percentage error, comment.

marking_scheme.step: Absolute error 0.13 g and percentage error 1.3 %

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between precision and accuracy. [2]

(b) Two students measure the density of a copper block, whose accepted value is 8.96 g cm⁻³. Student P records 8.91, 8.93, 8.92 g cm⁻³ and student Q records 9.30, 8.40, 8.95 g cm⁻³. Find each mean to three significant figures and state which student's work is more precise and which mean is closer to the accepted value. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Precision is the closeness of repeated measurements to one another; accuracy is the closeness of a measurement, or of the mean, to the true or accepted value. (b) Mean of P $= (8.91 + 8.93 + 8.92) / 3 = 8.92$ g cm⁻³; mean of Q $= (9.3 + 8.4 + 8.95) / 3 \approx 8.88$ g cm⁻³. P's readings span 0.02 g cm⁻³ and Q's span 0.90 g cm⁻³, so P is far more precise. P's mean differs from 8.96 by 0.04 and Q's by 0.08, so P's mean is also closer to the accepted value.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; two means; spread and distance from the accepted value.

questions.stem_md: Match each quantity with its unit expressed in SI base units.
questions.solution_md: Newton $= \text{kg m s}^{-2}$ (mass × acceleration); joule $= \text{N m} = \text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$; pascal $= \text{N m}^{-2} = \text{kg m}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-2}$; density is mass per volume, $\text{kg m}^{-3}$.

questions.stem_md: The pressure gauge of a gas cylinder reads $2.0 \times 10^{6}$ Pa. Taking 1 atm = $1.013 \times 10^{5}$ Pa, the pressure in atmospheres is about:
questions.solution_md: The conversion factor is $\dfrac{1\ \text{atm}}{1.013 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}}$, so the pressure is $2.0 \times 10^{6} \times \dfrac{1}{1.013 \times 10^{5}} \approx 20$ atm — option (a). (b) is off by a factor of ten; (c) uses the conversion factor upside down, and (d) multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem_md: A hospital drip bag holds 500 mL of saline. Its volume in m³ is:
questions.solution_md: $1\ \text{mL} = 1\ \text{cm}^3 = 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^3$, so $500 \times 10^{-6} = 5.00 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^3$ — option (b). (a) uses $10^{-9}$ per millilitre by mistake, and (c) treats the bag as 5 litres.

questions.stem_md: A bicycle tyre is inflated to 2.20 atm. With 1 atm = 101325 Pa, the pressure in pascal, to three significant figures, is:
questions.solution_md: $2.20 \times 101325 = 222915 \approx 2.23 \times 10^{5}\ \text{Pa}$ — option (d). (a) rounds the factor to $10^{5}$ and loses accuracy; (b) and (c) misplace the power of ten.

questions.stem_md: In SI base units, pressure is $\text{kg m}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-2}$ and volume is $\text{m}^{3}$. The product $PV$ therefore has the same dimensions as:
questions.solution_md: $PV$ has units $\text{kg m}^{-1}\text{ s}^{-2} \times \text{m}^{3} = \text{kg m}^{2}\text{ s}^{-2}$, which is the joule, the unit of energy — option (a). Force is $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$, momentum $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$ and power $\text{kg m}^{2}\text{ s}^{-3}$.

questions.stem_md: A goods train on a straight track moves at 54 km h⁻¹. Its speed in m s⁻¹ is:
questions.solution_md: $54\ \dfrac{\text{km}}{\text{h}} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{km}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{h}}{3600\ \text{s}} = 15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ — option (d). (a) multiplies by 3.6 instead of dividing, and (b) divides by 60 only.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A conversion factor such as 1 dm / 10 cm is equal to one, so multiplying by it changes the unit but not the size of the quantity.
questions.solution_md: True. The numerator and denominator are the same length expressed in different units, so the factor equals 1 and the physical quantity is unchanged.

questions.stem_md: One standard atmosphere is equal to ___ Pa (to four significant figures, in the form a × 10⁵).
questions.solution_md: By definition 1 atm = 101325 Pa, which is 1.013 × 10⁵ Pa to four significant figures.

questions.stem_md: A diver's gauge reads 3.50 atm. Using 1 atm = 101325 Pa, find the pressure in kPa, to three significant figures.
questions.solution_md: $3.50 \times 101325\ \text{Pa} = 354638\ \text{Pa}$, and dividing by 1000 gives $354.6$ kPa $\approx 355$ kPa.

questions.stem_md: The carbon–carbon bond length in graphite is 0.142 nm. Express it (i) in metres and (ii) in picometres.
questions.solution_md: Use 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m and 1 pm = 10⁻¹² m.

questions.stem_md: The engine of a scooter has a displacement of 149 cm³. A cooling pump delivers water at 2.4 L min⁻¹. Express (i) the displacement in dm³, (ii) the displacement in m³, and (iii) the flow rate in m³ s⁻¹.
questions.solution_md: Each conversion by a factor equal to one.

questions.stem_md: The density of mercury is 13.6 g cm⁻³. Convert it to kg m⁻³ and find the mass, in kilograms, of 250 mL of mercury filled in a barometer reservoir.

answer.model_answer_md: $13.6\ \dfrac{\text{g}}{\text{cm}^3} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{kg}}{10^{3}\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{10^{6}\ \text{cm}^3}{1\ \text{m}^3} = 1.36 \times 10^{4}\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$. Mass $= 13.6 \times 250 = 3400$ g $= 3.40$ kg.

questions.solution_md: Two conversion factors for the density; then mass = density × volume.

questions.stem_md:
(a) The gas constant is $R = 0.0821\ \text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$. Using 1 L = $10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3$ and 1 atm = 101325 Pa, express $R$ in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. [3]

(b) Show by dimensional analysis that the litre-atmosphere is a unit of energy. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $R = 0.0821 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3 \times 101325\ \text{Pa}\ \text{K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1} = 8.319$, that is $R \approx 8.32\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$, because $1\ \text{Pa m}^3 = 1\ \text{J}$. (b) $1\ \text{L atm} = 10^{-3}\ \text{m}^3 \times 101325\ \text{N m}^{-2} = 101.3\ \text{N m} = 101.3\ \text{J}$; pressure × volume has the dimensions of force × length, which is work or energy.

questions.solution_md: Convert L to m³ and atm to Pa; then Pa m³ = N m = J.

marking_scheme.step: (b) 1 L atm in SI units, about 101.3 J
(b) Pressure × volume has dimensions of force × length

questions.stem_md: In a sealed flask, 20.8 g of barium chloride and 14.2 g of sodium sulfate, both in solution, are mixed. 23.3 g of barium sulfate precipitates and the only other product is dissolved sodium chloride. The mass of sodium chloride formed is:
questions.solution_md: In a sealed flask nothing escapes, so mass of products equals mass of reactants: $20.8 + 14.2 = 35.0$ g. Sodium chloride $= 35.0 - 23.3 = 11.7$ g — option (b). (a) is the total mass of reactants, and (d) adds the precipitate to it.

questions.stem_md: A student burns 2.4 g of magnesium ribbon in an open crucible and finds the white ash weighs 3.98 g, which is more than the metal she started with. Which statement explains this correctly?

options.text_md: The ash contains oxygen taken from the air; mass of magnesium plus mass of oxygen used equals the mass of ash.
The law of conservation of mass does not hold for reactions in open vessels.
Magnesium atoms become heavier when heated.
Part of the magnesium was converted into oxygen.

questions.solution_md: Oxygen from the air combines with the metal, so the ash weighs more: the oxygen taken up is $3.98 - 2.4 = 1.58$ g. Counting the air that took part, mass is conserved — option (a). (b) is wrong because the law always holds when every substance is counted; (c) and (d) contradict Dalton's idea that atoms keep their identity.

questions.stem_md: Zinc oxide prepared by roasting zinc carbonate contains 4.01 g of zinc in a 5.00 g sample. Zinc oxide made by burning zinc metal contains 6.44 g of zinc in a 8.03 g sample. These data support the law of:
questions.solution_md: Zinc fraction in the first sample $= 4.01 / 5.00 = 0.802$; in the second $= 6.44 / 8.03 = 0.802$. The same compound from two sources has the same composition — option (b). Multiple and reciprocal proportions (a, c) need different compounds.

questions.stem_md: A 4.78 g sample of lead sulfide made in a laboratory contains 0.64 g of sulfur. A 11.95 g sample of the mineral galena contains 1.6 g of sulfur. Do the data agree with the law of definite proportions?

answer.model_answer_md: Sulfur per gram of sample: $0.64 / 4.78 = 0.1339$ and $1.6 / 11.95 = 0.1339$. The two values agree (13.4 % sulfur in each), so lead sulfide from both sources has the same composition by mass and the law of definite proportions is obeyed.

questions.solution_md: Compare the sulfur fractions of the two samples.

marking_scheme.step: Equal fractions, so the law is obeyed

questions.stem_md: In an open beaker, 2.65 g of anhydrous sodium carbonate is stirred with 4.2 g of dilute hydrochloric acid. Carbon dioxide escapes and the beaker with its contents is found to have lost 1.1 g. What mass of material is left in the beaker? Which law is illustrated?

answer.model_answer_md: Total mass before $= 2.65 + 4.2 = 6.85$ g. The mass after must be the same once the escaped gas is counted, so the beaker holds $6.85 - 1.1 = 5.75$ g. This illustrates the law of conservation of mass: the escaped carbon dioxide accounts for the apparent loss.

questions.solution_md: Mass before minus mass of escaped gas.

questions.stem_md: Phosphorus forms two chlorides. In the first, 1.00 g of phosphorus combines with 3.44 g of chlorine; in the second, 1.00 g of phosphorus combines with 5.73 g. The ratio of the masses of chlorine that combine with a fixed mass of phosphorus is:
questions.solution_md: $3.44 : 5.73 = 1 : 1.67$, and $0.60 \approx 3/5$, so the ratio is $3 : 5$ — option (c), as expected for $\ce{PCl3}$ and $\ce{PCl5}$. This is the law of multiple proportions.

questions.stem_md: A steel-plant chemist analyses two oxides of iron. Oxide X contains 77.7 % iron by mass and oxide Y contains 70.0 % iron. (i) Find the mass of oxygen combined with 1.00 g of iron in each oxide. (ii) Show that the two masses are in a simple ratio. (iii) Name and state the law illustrated.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Oxide X: $(100 - 77.7) / 77.7 = 0.287$ g oxygen per gram of iron; oxide Y: $(100 - 70.0) / 70.0 = 0.429$ g. (ii) $0.287 : 0.429 = 2 : 3$ (the ratio is 0.67). (iii) This is the law of multiple proportions: when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio.

questions.solution_md: Oxygen per gram of iron; the ratio 2 : 3; statement of the law.

questions.stem_md: A teacher lists four laboratory records on the board. Pair every law on the left with the record that demonstrates it.

match_right.text_md: Copper forms two chlorides in which 1.00 g of copper combines with 0.559 g and 1.118 g of chlorine
A sealed flask weighs 85.20 g before and after a precipitation reaction inside it
Pure water from any source gives 8.0 g of oxygen for every 1.0 g of hydrogen
60 mL of hydrogen reacts with 20 mL of nitrogen to give 40 mL of ammonia at the same temperature and pressure

questions.solution_md: Equal mass before and after is conservation; the same composition in two sources is definite proportions; $0.559 : 1.118 = 1 : 2$ is multiple proportions; $60 : 20 : 40 = 3 : 1 : 2$ is a simple volume ratio, Gay-Lussac's law.

questions.stem_md: Proust’s law states that a pure compound always contains the same elements combined in the same mass ratio; it is called the law of ___ proportions.
questions.solution_md: The law of **definite** (constant) proportions.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the law of multiple proportions. [1]

(b) Copper forms two chlorides. In one, 6.35 g of copper is combined with 3.55 g of chlorine; in the other, 6.35 g of copper is combined with 7.10 g of chlorine. Calculate the mass of chlorine combined with 1.00 g of copper in each, and show that the data obey the law. [2]

(c) A 4.78 g sample of lead sulfide made in a laboratory contains 0.64 g of sulfur and a 11.95 g sample of galena contains 1.60 g of sulfur. Which law do these data illustrate? Show your working. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) When two elements combine to form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a simple whole-number ratio. (b) First chloride: $3.55 / 6.35 = 0.559$ g Cl per gram of Cu; second: $7.10 / 6.35 = 1.118$ g. The ratio $0.559 : 1.118 = 1 : 2$, a simple whole-number ratio, so the law is obeyed. (c) Sulfur fractions: $0.64 / 4.78 = 0.134$ and $1.60 / 11.95 = 0.134$. The same compound has the same composition from both sources: the law of definite proportions.

questions.solution_md: Statement; two ratios and 1 : 2; equal fractions for lead sulfide.

marking_scheme.step: (b) 0.559 g and 1.118 g per gram of Cu

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When a candle burns in a sealed bottle, the total mass of the bottle and its contents does not change.

**Reason (R):** Atoms are rearranged during a chemical reaction; they are neither created nor destroyed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true because nothing enters or leaves the sealed bottle (law of conservation of mass). R is true and is exactly the reason: the same atoms are present before and after, only rearranged — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In ammonia, 3.00 g of hydrogen combines with 14.0 g of nitrogen. In water, 3.00 g of hydrogen combines with 24.0 g of oxygen. In dinitrogen trioxide, 14.0 g of nitrogen combines directly with 24.0 g of oxygen. These data verify the law of:
questions.solution_md: Through the common element hydrogen, N : O $= 14 : 24 = 7 : 12$. The direct ratio in the oxide is $14 : 24 = 7 : 12$, the same — the law of reciprocal proportions, option (c). Multiple proportions (a) compares two compounds of the same two elements.

questions.stem_md: In hydrogen sulfide, 1.00 g of hydrogen combines with 16.0 g of sulfur; in water, 1.00 g of hydrogen combines with 8.00 g of oxygen. In sulfur trioxide, sulfur and oxygen combine directly in the mass ratio 2 : 3. Compared with the ratio S : O obtained through hydrogen, the direct ratio is:

options.text_md: one third of it, a simple fraction

questions.solution_md: Through hydrogen, S : O $= 16 : 8 = 2$. Direct, S : O $= 2 : 3 = 0.667$. The direct ratio divided by the ratio through hydrogen is $0.667 / 2 = 0.333 \approx 1/3$ — option (c). A simple multiple or fraction is what the law of reciprocal proportions allows.

questions.stem_md: Methane contains 12.0 g of carbon combined with 4.00 g of hydrogen; carbon tetrachloride contains 12.0 g of carbon combined with 142 g of chlorine; hydrogen chloride contains 1.00 g of hydrogen combined with 35.5 g of chlorine. (i) What masses of hydrogen and chlorine combine with 12.0 g of carbon? (ii) Find the ratio H : Cl through carbon. (iii) Compare it with the direct ratio in hydrogen chloride and name the law.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) 4.00 g of hydrogen and 142 g of chlorine. (ii) H : Cl $= 4.00 : 142 = 1 : 35.5$ $(0.0282)$. (iii) In hydrogen chloride, H : Cl $= 1.00 : 35.5 = 1 : 35.5$ $(0.0282)$, which is the same. Two elements that each combine with a third combine with each other in the same ratio (or a simple multiple of it): the law of reciprocal proportions.

questions.solution_md: Masses with fixed carbon; ratio 1 : 35.5; same as direct ratio.

marking_scheme.step: (i) 4.00 g H and 142 g Cl with 12.0 g C

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the law of reciprocal proportions, the ratio in which two elements combine with a fixed mass of a third element is the same as, or a simple multiple of, the ratio in which they combine with each other.

**Reason (R):** The law of reciprocal proportions is another name for the law of multiple proportions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is a correct statement of the law (Richter). R is false: multiple proportions compares two compounds of the same pair of elements, whereas reciprocal proportions compares the combining ratios of two elements through a third — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the law of reciprocal proportions. [1]

(b) Sodium chloride has 2.30 g of sodium combined with 3.55 g of chlorine, and sodium oxide has 2.30 g of sodium combined with 0.8 g of oxygen. Find the ratio of the masses of chlorine and oxygen that combine with 2.30 g of sodium. [2]

(c) In dichlorine monoxide, 7.1 g of chlorine is combined directly with 1.6 g of oxygen. Show that the data obey the law of reciprocal proportions. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) If two elements combine separately with a fixed mass of a third element, the masses in which they do so are in the same ratio, or a simple multiple of it, as the masses in which they combine with each other. (b) With 2.30 g of sodium: 3.55 g of chlorine and 0.8 g of oxygen, so Cl : O $= 3.55 : 0.8 = 4.44 : 1$. (c) Directly in the oxide, Cl : O $= 7.1 : 1.6 = 4.44 : 1$. The two ratios are identical (the simple multiple is 1), so the data obey the law of reciprocal proportions.

questions.solution_md: Statement; ratio 4.44 : 1 through sodium; same ratio in the oxide.

questions.stem_md: A chemist burns 20 mL of ethyne in 70 mL of oxygen: $\ce{2C2H2 + 5O2 -> 4CO2 + 2H2O}$. The products are cooled to the original temperature and pressure, when the water is liquid. The volume of the gas mixture is then:
questions.solution_md: By Gay-Lussac's law the gas volumes react as $2 : 5 : 4$. 20 mL of ethyne uses 50 mL of oxygen and gives 40 mL of $\ce{CO2}$; oxygen left $= 70 - 50 = 20$ mL. Gas volume $= 40 + 20 = 60$ mL — option (c). (a) is the volume before the reaction, (b) counts only the carbon dioxide and (d) counts only the oxygen left.

questions.stem_md: 30 mL of nitrogen and 60 mL of hydrogen are passed over a catalyst: $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$. Reaction goes to completion at constant temperature and pressure. The total volume of gas at the end is:
questions.solution_md: Volumes react as $1 : 3 : 2$. Hydrogen is limiting: 60 mL of it uses 20 mL of nitrogen and gives 40 mL of ammonia. Nitrogen left $= 30 - 20 = 10$ mL, so the total is $40 + 10 = 50$ mL — option (b). (d) forgets the unused nitrogen.

questions.stem_md: At constant temperature and pressure, $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$. What volume of ammonia, in mL, is obtained from 90 mL of hydrogen with excess nitrogen?
questions.solution_md: Hydrogen and ammonia are in the volume ratio $3 : 2$, so $V = 90 \times 2/3 = 60$ mL.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Gay-Lussac’s law of combining volumes applies equally to gaseous, liquid and solid reactants measured at the same temperature.
questions.solution_md: False. The law applies to gases only: it relates the volumes of gaseous reactants and gaseous products measured at the same temperature and pressure.

questions.stem_md: 30 mL of carbon monoxide is burnt completely in air: $\ce{2CO + O2 -> 2CO2}$. All volumes are at the same temperature and pressure. Find the volumes of oxygen consumed and carbon dioxide formed, and name the law used.

answer.model_answer_md: The volumes are in the ratio $2 : 1 : 2$ (Gay-Lussac's law). Oxygen used $= 30 / 2 = 15$ mL; carbon dioxide formed $= 30$ mL.

questions.solution_md: Volume ratio 2 : 1 : 2.

marking_scheme.step: Oxygen 15 mL and carbon dioxide 30 mL

questions.stem_md: 20 mL of propane is burnt in 150 mL of oxygen: $\ce{C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O}$. The products are cooled to the original temperature and pressure, when the water is liquid. Find (i) the volume of oxygen consumed, (ii) the volume of carbon dioxide formed and (iii) the total volume of gas remaining.

answer.model_answer_md: Gas volumes react as $1 : 5 : 3$. (i) Oxygen used $= 5 \times 20 = 100$ mL. (ii) $\ce{CO2}$ formed $= 3 \times 20 = 60$ mL. (iii) Oxygen left $= 150 - 100 = 50$ mL, so the gas remaining is $60 + 50 = 110$ mL.

questions.solution_md: Use the volume ratio 1 : 5 : 3.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Gases react in simple whole-number ratios of volume when measured at the same temperature and pressure.

**Reason (R):** Gay-Lussac’s law of combining volumes was fully explained by Dalton’s atomic theory.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is a correct statement of Gay-Lussac’s law. R is false: Dalton assumed that elementary gases were single atoms and could not account for the volume ratios; Avogadro’s molecular hypothesis was needed — option (c).

questions.stem_md: One volume of hydrogen and one volume of chlorine give two volumes of hydrogen chloride at the same temperature and pressure. Avogadro explained this by proposing that:

options.text_md: molecules of hydrogen and of chlorine each contain two atoms, which separate on reaction
one volume of any gas holds one atom of that gas
a hydrogen chloride molecule has one hydrogen atom and two chlorine atoms
hydrogen and chlorine atoms cannot combine in equal numbers

questions.solution_md: Equal volumes hold equal numbers of molecules. If $\ce{H2}$ and $\ce{Cl2}$ are diatomic, one molecule of each gives two molecules of $\ce{HCl}$: $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$, so 1 + 1 volumes give 2 volumes — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
(a) State Gay-Lussac's law of combining volumes. [1]

(b) 40 mL of hydrogen is mixed with 25 mL of oxygen and ignited: $\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$. The mixture is cooled to the original temperature and pressure, when the water is liquid. Which gas is left over and what is its volume? [2]

(c) One volume of hydrogen and one volume of chlorine give two volumes of hydrogen chloride. Using Avogadro's law, show that this requires the molecules of hydrogen and chlorine to be diatomic. [2]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Gases react with one another, and form gaseous products, in volumes that bear a simple whole-number ratio, when all volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. (b) Hydrogen and oxygen react in the volume ratio $2 : 1$, so 40 mL of hydrogen needs 20 mL of oxygen. Oxygen left $= 25 - 20 = 5$ mL, and since water is a liquid the only gas remaining is 5 mL of oxygen. (c) By Avogadro's law, equal volumes contain equal numbers of molecules. If $n$ molecules of hydrogen react with $n$ molecules of chlorine, $2n$ molecules of hydrogen chloride form. Each molecule of hydrogen chloride needs at least one atom of each element, so each hydrogen and chlorine molecule must supply two atoms: $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$.

questions.solution_md: Law; oxygen in excess; Avogadro argument.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Law stated with same T and P
(c) Equal numbers of molecules from equal volumes
(c) Two molecules of HCl need two atoms of each element: diatomic

questions.stem_md: Which of the following observations is not consistent with Dalton’s original postulate that all atoms of an element are identical in mass?

options.text_md: Water from any source contains hydrogen and oxygen in the mass ratio 1 : 8
Neon exists as atoms of mass numbers 20, 21 and 22
Carbon and oxygen form both carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide
The mass of a closed system is the same before and after a reaction

questions.solution_md: The existence of isotopes (neon-20, neon-21, neon-22) shows atoms of one element can differ in mass — option (b). The other three observations are consistent with, and were explained by, Dalton’s theory.

questions.stem_md: Which discovery most directly contradicted Dalton’s postulate that atoms are indivisible?

options.text_md: Cathode-ray tubes yielded electrons from atoms of every gas used
Proust’s analysis of two samples of copper carbonate
Gay-Lussac’s measurement of combining volumes of gases
Lavoisier’s weighing of mercury before and after heating

questions.solution_md: Identical negatively charged particles (electrons) came from atoms of every gas, so atoms must have smaller constituents — option (a). The other three experiments led to laws that Dalton’s theory explained.

questions.stem_md: A student lists the particles of four substances. Which entry is a molecule of an element?
questions.solution_md: A molecule of an element contains atoms of one kind only. White phosphorus has four phosphorus atoms per molecule — option (d). The other three molecules contain two different elements, so they are molecules of compounds.

questions.stem_md: Which postulate of Dalton’s atomic theory is the direct basis for the law of conservation of mass?

options.text_md: Atoms of different elements differ in mass and properties.
Atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; they are only rearranged.
Atoms combine in small whole-number ratios to form compounds.
All the atoms of an element are identical.

questions.solution_md: If atoms are only rearranged, the number and mass of atoms are unchanged by a reaction, so total mass is conserved — option (b). Small whole-number ratios explain the laws of definite and multiple proportions.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** According to Dalton, an atom can be broken into smaller particles during a chemical reaction.

**Reason (R):** Dalton’s theory explains the existence of isotopes of an element.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are false. Dalton’s atom was indivisible and was only rearranged in reactions, and his postulate that all atoms of an element are identical in mass rules out isotopes — option (d).

questions.stem_md: State any two postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory. Which one of them has been modified by later discoveries, and how?

answer.model_answer_md: Postulates: (1) matter consists of indivisible atoms; (2) atoms of an element are identical in mass and properties; (3) atoms combine in small whole-number ratios to form compounds; (4) atoms are neither created nor destroyed in reactions. The postulate that atoms of an element are identical in mass is modified: isotopes of one element have different masses.

questions.solution_md: Two postulates and one modification.

questions.stem_md: Give two limitations of Dalton’s atomic theory, each supported by an observation that contradicts it.

answer.model_answer_md: First, atoms are divisible: electrons, protons and neutrons are found inside atoms. Second, atoms of one element are not all identical in mass: chlorine consists of isotopes of mass numbers 35 and 37. (Other limitations: the theory could not explain Gay-Lussac’s law, and does not explain why diamond and graphite, both made of carbon atoms, differ in properties.)

questions.solution_md: Two limitations with evidence.

questions.stem_md: Use Dalton’s postulates to explain (i) the law of conservation of mass, (ii) the law of definite proportions and (iii) the law of multiple proportions, taking carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide as the example for (iii).

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Atoms are only rearranged, never created or destroyed, so the total mass of reactants equals that of products. (ii) A compound is made of atoms combined in a fixed whole-number ratio and every atom of an element has the same mass, so the mass ratio of the elements is always the same. (iii) The same atoms can combine in different whole-number ratios: carbon monoxide has one oxygen atom per carbon atom and carbon dioxide has two, so for a fixed mass of carbon the masses of oxygen are in the ratio 1 : 2.

questions.stem_md: Explain why Dalton’s theory could not account for Gay-Lussac’s observation that 1 volume of hydrogen and 1 volume of chlorine give 2 volumes of hydrogen chloride, and state how Avogadro resolved the difficulty.

answer.model_answer_md: Dalton took the smallest particle of a gaseous element to be a single atom. With one atom of hydrogen and one of chlorine, equal volumes would give one particle of hydrogen chloride per pair, and so only one volume of product, not two. Avogadro proposed that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure hold equal numbers of molecules and that hydrogen and chlorine exist as diatomic molecules; each molecule splits into two atoms, giving two molecules of hydrogen chloride and so two volumes.

questions.solution_md: Dalton’s monatomic assumption; Avogadro’s molecules.

questions.stem_md:
(a) State two postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory and show how they explain the law of conservation of mass. [2]

(b) Describe three limitations of the theory, giving for each the later discovery that shows it. [3]

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Matter is made of atoms that cannot be created or destroyed in a chemical reaction; a reaction only rearranges atoms into new combinations. Because the number and kind of atoms, each with a fixed mass, are unchanged, the total mass of the reactants equals that of the products. (b) First, atoms are divisible: the discovery of the electron, proton and neutron shows they have internal structure. Second, atoms of the same element can differ in mass: isotopes such as chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 exist. Third, the theory treats the smallest particle of a gas as an atom, so it fails to explain Gay-Lussac’s law; Avogadro’s concept of the molecule was needed. (Also, it cannot explain allotropy: diamond and graphite, both carbon, differ in properties.)

questions.solution_md: Two postulates and conservation of mass; three limitations with evidence.
